toc.title: Scope and Quality (PMBOK 8 link; detail in Topic 18)
Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

html:
1Core Concepts and Definitions

Purpose of the domain: make sure the project includes all the work required, and only the work required, so that cost and schedule are optimized and value is maximized. PMBOK 8 also gives this domain a quality focus: scope is the outcome delivered, and quality is meeting stakeholder expectations and requirements.

Term Meaning
Scope The sum of the products, services and results the project provides
Product scope The features, functions and characteristics of the product, service or result: what it should look like and do
Project scope The work performed to deliver a product, service or result with the specified features and functions
Requirement A condition or capability that must be present in a product, service or result to satisfy a business need
Deliverable Any unique and verifiable product, result or capability to perform a service that must be produced to complete a process, phase or project (tangible or intangible; includes project documentation)
Scope baseline (predictive) The approved project scope statement + WBS + WBS dictionary, changeable only through formal change control. With the schedule and cost baselines it forms the performance measurement baseline (PMB)
Scope baseline (adaptive) Defined at the start of each iteration and aligned with prioritized requirements by expected value; usually the product owner approves changes dynamically, without formal change control
WBS A hierarchical decomposition of the total scope into deliverables and work packages
Work package / planning package / control account Work package: lowest WBS level, with a unique ID, whose cost and duration can be estimated and managed. Control account: a management control point where scope, budget and schedule are integrated (at least two work packages). Planning package: below a control account, with known content but no detailed activities yet
Acceptance criteria The conditions that must be met before deliverables are accepted
Definition of done (DoD) A checklist of criteria a deliverable (story, feature or increment) must meet to be ready for the customer or the next stage
Product backlog A dynamic, prioritized list of work items and features (kept by the product owner); the release backlog and iteration backlog are subsets
Epic / feature / user story Epic: large body of related work organizing requirements and delivering business outcomes. Feature: related requirements that provide value. User story: a brief statement of an outcome from a stakeholder's perspective (role, goal, motivation) and a promise for a conversation
Minimum viable product (MVP) The fewest features or requirements that deliver value in a first release
Value breakdown structure (VBS) A hierarchy linking project scope and intended value to the product scope that creates it. Top-level deliverables carry a value estimate (a number or a percentage of total value; 100% if mandatory), which helps prioritize work and estimate the drag cost of critical-path items
Scope creep Uncontrolled expansion of scope without adjustments to time, cost and resources
Gold plating Beyond PMBOK 8 Adding unrequested features or extras beyond the agreed scope; a form of unapproved scope growth
Verification / validation Verification: does the deliverable comply with the requirement, specification or imposed condition? Validation: does it meet the needs of the customer and other stakeholders?

2The Six Scope Processes

Process Focus area Purpose Key outputs Decision tools
Plan Scope Management Planning Define how project and product scope will be defined, validated and controlled; remove work that adds no value Scope management plan, requirements management plan Expert judgment, data gathering (interviews, focus groups, surveys), data analysis, test and inspection planning
Elicit and Analyze Requirements Planning Determine, document and manage stakeholder needs and requirements; in adaptive work, capture them as user stories in a prioritized backlog Requirements documentation Expert judgment, decision-making, data gathering (benchmarking, brainstorming, focus groups, interviews, surveys), document analysis, nominal group, design thinking, prioritization/ranking, meetings
Define Scope Planning Describe the project, the product and the expected value in detail (predictive: at the start) or at a high level (adaptive: product roadmap with releases; at the start of each iteration); identify quality requirements and standards and how compliance will be shown Project scope statement Expert judgment, decision-making, data analysis, decomposition, facilitation, product analysis
Develop Scope Structure Planning Subdivide deliverables and work into manageable components; adaptive: break the backlog into epics, features and user stories Scope baseline (scope statement, WBS, WBS dictionary); user stories; product backlog Expert judgment, brainstorming, decomposition
Monitor and Control Scope Monitoring & Controlling Track scope status, manage changes to the scope baseline, measure the quality of deliverables and confirm standards are met Verified deliverables, quality reports, quality control measurements, change requests, work performance information Variance, trend and root cause analysis, performance reviews, audits and inspections, testing / product evaluations, process automation
Validate Scope Monitoring & Controlling Check the processes used to reach quality standards and formalize acceptance of completed deliverables Accepted deliverables, change requests Data gathering and analysis, inspection, decision-making, customer talks and tests, process analysis, review meetings

3Plan Scope Management

The scope management plan (a component of the project management plan) is formal or informal, broad or detailed, and describes:

  1. How the project scope statement is prepared
  2. How the WBS is created from the detailed scope statement
  3. How the scope baseline is approved and maintained
  4. How formal acceptance of completed deliverables is obtained

The requirements management plan (some organizations call it a business analysis plan) describes how requirements are analyzed, documented and managed: planning, tracking and reporting of requirements work; configuration management (how changes are initiated, how impacts are analyzed, how changes are traced and reported, authorization levels); the prioritization process; metrics; and the traceability structure used in the requirements traceability matrix.

The objective, delivering value, is the same in every approach, but adaptive scope management is more iterative and collaborative. The plan is built around the life cycle.

4Elicit and Analyze Requirements

Requirements documentation may start high level and become more detailed. Before baselining, a requirement should be unambiguous (measurable and testable), traceable, complete, consistent and acceptable to key stakeholders. The format ranges from a simple list sorted by stakeholder and priority to a full document.

4.1 Elicitation techniques

Technique Notes
Interviews Direct, individual; ideal for experienced participants, sponsors, executives and experts, and for confidential information
Focus groups Prequalified stakeholders and experts, led by a moderator in a conversational discussion
Questionnaires and surveys Many respondents, dispersed audiences, quick turnaround, statistical analysis
Observation / conversation (job shadowing) Watch people do their work; best when users cannot or will not articulate needs; uncovers hidden requirements (a "participant observer" performs the process)
Benchmarking Compare with comparable organizations to find good practices and ideas
Brainstorming, mind mapping, affinity diagram Generate ideas; consolidate and group them
Nominal group Structured: everyone contributes ideas before discussion; equalizes participation, limits dominant voices
Document analysis Contracts, policies, process flows, regulations, issue logs, test and quality reports, use cases
Design thinking Human-centered and iterative: define the problem, ideate, prototype, test
Prototypes A working model that gets early feedback before building the product
Prioritization / ranking MoSCoW (must, should, could, will not have), 100-point method, cost of delay, Kano analysis; stakeholders themselves can also be ranked (Topic 10)
Decision-making Voting, autocratic, multicriteria analysis (Topic 14)

4.2 Practical rules

  • Conflicting requirements: make the conflict visible to everyone involved and discuss trade-offs together. Ranking or picking the senior person's request leaves others surprised later.
  • Vague goal ("improve engagement"): agree measurable outcomes with stakeholders first; acceptance criteria follow from them.
  • Signed requirements, different expectations: the document cannot settle it; facilitate a discussion to align the parties.
  • Hidden or assumed expectations: surface them early (observation, interviews, prototypes).
  • Compliance and sustainability requirements are requirements: confirm them early and put them in the backlog or scope (Topics 07 and 23). A customer-required sustainability criterion (for example water-use certification) is a quality requirement.
  • Adaptive: requirements arrive as user stories with acceptance criteria, ordered in a backlog; the conversation matters more than the document. Beyond PMBOK 8 "INVEST" (independent, negotiable, valuable, estimable, small, testable) is a common checklist for good stories.

4.3 Requirements traceability matrix (RTM)

A grid that links each requirement from its origin to the deliverable that satisfies it (and onward to design, test and acceptance). It shows that every approved requirement is delivered, that each one adds business value (it links to a business or project objective), and it structures change management of product scope. Typical attributes: ID, source, priority, owner, status, acceptance criteria.

Requirements with no linked objective [Beyond PMBOK 8 — exam practice]: the matrix exists to show value, so an unlinked requirement is a question, not a formatting gap. Confirm with the stakeholders whether it belongs in scope (keep with a stated objective, or remove it). Do not attach it to the "closest" objective just to complete the matrix, because that fakes traceability.

5Define Scope

Project scope statement (detailed description of the project and product scope; common understanding among stakeholders; baseline for judging whether a request is inside or outside the project's boundaries):

Element Content
Scope description Progressive elaboration of the product, service or result in the charter and requirements
Deliverables Unique, verifiable products, results or capabilities, including ancillary ones such as reports and documentation
Acceptance criteria Conditions that must be met before deliverables are accepted
Exclusions What is out of scope; managing expectations and reducing scope creep
Assumptions and constraints Recorded with the scope (and in the assumption log)
  • Charter vs scope statement: the charter has high-level information; the scope statement is the detailed description, progressively elaborated (Topic 09).
  • Product analysis turns a high-level product description into deliverables: product breakdown, requirements analysis, systems analysis, systems engineering, value analysis, value engineering.
  • Quality: Define Scope identifies the quality requirements and standards for deliverables and how compliance will be demonstrated (Topic 18).
  • Adaptive: scope is described at a high level, typically the product roadmap with its releases, and re-defined at the start of each iteration. An MVP can focus the first release on the fewest features that deliver value.

Obtaining stakeholder agreement on scope (ECO enabler):

  1. Review the scope statement, requirements, exclusions and acceptance criteria with the key stakeholders and sponsor.
  2. Surface and resolve conflicting or unstated expectations before the scope is approved or baselined.
  3. Obtain documented approval; the approved documents form the baseline.
  4. In adaptive work, agree the vision, MVP, prioritization criteria and definition of done at planning events; the product owner is the voice for scope decisions, and stakeholder feedback is built into each iteration.

6Develop Scope Structure

Predictive: the WBS states the objectives and defines the deliverables in a hierarchy of manageable work packages that can be assigned, tracked and measured, giving a shared understanding and clear ownership.

Rule Detail
100% rule The WBS contains all product and project work (including project management work) and nothing more; the lowest levels roll up to the higher ones
Decomposition Identify deliverables and related work; structure the WBS; decompose upper levels; assign IDs (code of accounts); check that the degree of decomposition is appropriate
Right depth Components must be necessary and sufficient for the parent deliverable and estimable, assignable and controllable. Different deliverables can have different depths. Too much decomposition causes wasted effort and roll-up problems
Rolling wave Far-future work that cannot be decomposed yet stays as a planning package and is detailed later
How to build it Top-down, from organizational guidelines or templates; bottom-up grouping is possible; levels by life cycle phase or by major deliverable; contracted work gets its own contract WBS from the seller
Deliverable-oriented Branches name what is produced; activities come later (Topic 16)

WBS dictionary (for complex or interdependent deliverables): code of accounts identifier, description of work, assumptions and constraints, responsible organization, schedule milestones, associated activities, resources, cost estimates, quality requirements, acceptance criteria, technical references, agreement information.

Adaptive: the product backlog corresponds to the WBS; work items break down into epics, features and user stories, ordered by value. VBS (PMBOK 8) lets a team rank deliverables by their expected value.

7Monitor and Control Scope

Compares actual results with the baseline (or backlog), manages changes to the baseline, and measures the quality and value of deliverables.

7.1 Creep, elaboration and gold plating: what to do

Situation Is it a scope change? Right response
More detail as understanding grows, inside the agreed scope (progressive elaboration) No Update documents; no change request
Work already in the signed contract or scope statement but missing from the WBS No, it is in scope Add it to the WBS; no change request needed
A stakeholder asks for a new feature Yes, if it is outside the baseline Predictive: change request, impact assessment, approval (Topic 29). Adaptive: the product owner prioritizes it in the backlog
Team adds an unrequested extra "to delight the customer" (gold plating) Beyond PMBOK 8term Yes, unapproved Do not deliver it unapproved; if it is valuable, request it through change control
Vendor delivers more capacity or a better item than specified, at no cost A deviation Evaluate the impact (power, piping, safety, testing) and process it through change control
Executive asks for an urgent addition mid-iteration A backlog item Route to the product owner, show the trade-offs and capacity; protect the committed iteration unless the team and product owner agree a swap

7.2 Tools and metrics

  • Variance analysis (baseline vs actual, cause and degree), trend analysis, root cause analysis, performance reviews, audits and inspections, testing / product evaluations (Topic 28).
  • Adaptive: backlog management (the product owner ranks by value and the team sizes the items) and backlog refinement (progressive elaboration and reprioritization of the backlog); a burnup chart shows scope added versus work completed, so growing scope is not mistaken for a slow team.
  • PMBOK 8 Table 2-6 scope metrics: Scope definition accuracy (%) = planned scope items correctly delivered ÷ total planned scope items × 100. Scope creep (%) and requirements stability (%) are also given, but as printed they are upside down (total ÷ unplanned; total ÷ unchanged). The meaningful forms are unplanned ÷ total deliverables and unchanged ÷ total requirements, each × 100.
  • Contract thresholds in adaptive work: change control can be tailored. Routine backlog changes flow normally; changes above a contractual threshold (for example, a percentage of effort) need formal approval.

8Validate Scope

Two objectives: check the processes used to reach quality standards, and formalize acceptance of deliverables. The key benefit is an objective check that raises the probability of acceptance.

Verify (Monitor and Control Scope) Validate (Validate Scope)
Question Is it built correctly: does it comply with the requirement, specification and quality standard? Is it what the customer needs, and do they accept it?
Who Project team and quality function Customer, sponsor or the authorized acceptor
Output Verified deliverables (plus quality reports, measurements) Accepted deliverables (formal, documented)
If it fails Defect repair, then re-inspect Change request or rework; acceptance withheld
  • Quality control passed does not equal accepted. After verification, hold a formal acceptance review against the acceptance criteria that were defined up front.
  • Tools: inspection (reviews, walkthroughs, audits), customer talks and tests, review meetings, data gathering and analysis, decision-making.
  • Transition readiness matters: scope can be complete while the receiving team is not ready (for example support training). Validate readiness before handover (Topic 35).
  • Accepted deliverables feed Close Project or Phase; each phase closes formally even if the same sponsor continues.
  • Adaptive: sprint reviews or demos validate each increment against its definition of done and the acceptance criteria of its stories; early prototypes expose mismatches between a spec and what users expected.

9Scope and Quality (PMBOK 8 link; detail in Topic 18)

  • Quality is a feature of scope: functional and nonfunctional requirements and target thresholds (for a bridge: sturdiness, lifespan, maintainability) are scope, and they trade off with cost and schedule like any other scope.
  • Define Scope captures quality requirements and standards; Monitor and Control Scope measures quality and verifies deliverables; Validate Scope checks quality processes and obtains acceptance.
  • Sustainability in scope: the WBS or backlog should include work to manage sustainability, such as assessing and managing the project's CO₂ emissions or its impact on local biodiversity (Topic 07).

10Predictive vs Agile vs Hybrid

Predictive Agile / adaptive Hybrid
Scope definition Detailed up front: scope statement, requirements High level: vision, roadmap, MVP; detailed one iteration at a time Baseline for the fixed envelope; backlog for the evolving parts
Requirements Requirements documentation and RTM User stories with acceptance criteria, in a backlog Both, linked
Structure WBS and WBS dictionary Product backlog (epics, features, stories) WBS at upper levels, backlog beneath
Baseline Scope baseline changed through formal change control Baseline per iteration; product owner approves changes Baseline for milestones and committed scope; backlog adapts inside it
Prioritization Mandatory vs optional, by requirement priority By value, reordered continually (MoSCoW, cost of delay, Kano) Value-ordered backlog inside fixed constraints
Acceptance Formal acceptance against acceptance criteria Definition of done; sprint review; frequent customer feedback Per increment plus formal milestone acceptance
Flex Scope fixed, change is costly Fix time and cost, flex scope (prioritized increments) Fix the date, flex the content
Beyond PMBOK 8 INVEST criteria for stories; definition of ready

11Tailoring, Interactions and Checking Results

Tailoring considerations (PMBOK 8 §2.2.3):

Consideration What to do
Dependency on external partners Align scope with contractual agreements early; harmonize scope-related commitments of suppliers and subcontractors
Environmental dynamics In fast-changing markets and technologies, keep scope flexible with iterative feedback loops
Design phase Industries such as pharmaceuticals and construction invest heavily in early scope definition to avoid costly late change
Adaptive and hybrid life cycles Adaptive scope is refined over iterations; hybrid projects hold baselines for overall expectations while sub-teams iterate on backlog stories, which needs extra tailoring

PMBOK 8 examples: (1) a new product built from a backlog: the team delivers the main product goals, not every story on the list; (2) a mobile app in a new market with little customer information: an iterative approach with a clear MVP and rapid feedback; (3) a city park with a tight timeline and many stakeholders: invest more time in design and mock-ups before building.

Interactions: scope drives value and is the first baseline. A scope change hits schedule and finance immediately, so changes follow the governance structures (Topic 12). Risk: risk analysis shows effects on scope, and rescoping can be a risk response (mitigate, avoid or transfer). Stakeholders: requirements and acceptance come from them (Topic 13).

Check results (Table 2-6):

Outcome Check
Effective change management Predictive: a change log showing impact on all domains. Adaptive: backlog shows rate of scope done, rate of scope added, and stakeholder feedback included
Clear understanding of requirements Predictive: few changes to the initial requirements. Evolving: each iteration clarifies short-term requirements (rolling wave)
Alignment with business objectives Business case, strategic plan and authorizing documents match the deliverables
Stakeholders accept and are satisfied Interviews, observation, feedback; complaints and returns
Scope clearly defined Scope definition accuracy (%)
Scope creep measured Unplanned deliverables ÷ total (see note above)
Requirements stable Unchanged requirements ÷ total
Sustainability considered WBS or backlog includes sustainability work

12Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

  1. Already in the agreed scope but missing from the WBS? Add it. No change request is needed because it is not a change.
  2. A change request is for work outside the baseline. Do not process an in-scope omission as a change, and do not implement an out-of-scope request just because someone senior asked.
  3. Verified is not accepted. Quality control confirms correctness; the customer must formally accept against the acceptance criteria.
  4. Define acceptance criteria and exclusions up front. Vague goals need measurable outcomes before building.
  5. Make conflicting requirements visible and resolve them together. Do not just rank them or pick one.
  6. Signed requirements that people read differently call for a facilitated discussion, not another read of the document.
  7. No gold plating. Extras are not free: they add risk, testing and maintenance. A free upgrade still goes through impact assessment and change control.
  8. Decompose to the right level. Work packages must be estimable and controllable; do not detail far-future work (planning package and rolling wave) and do not leave deliverables undecomposed.
  9. The WBS covers 100% of the scope, including project management work, and nothing outside it.
  10. Traceability: use the RTM to show every approved requirement is delivered and every deliverable has a source. A requirement with no business objective is confirmed with stakeholders, not force-linked.
  11. Agile scope: route new requests to the backlog; the product owner prioritizes by value. Do not accept mid-iteration additions silently, and do not hide the trade-off.
  12. Definition of done includes tests, documentation and compliance; agree it with the team and product owner, not unilaterally.
  13. Fixed date, uncertain scope: fix the date and deliver prioritized increments; do not freeze uncertain scope to "guarantee" a date.
  14. External changes (market, regulation) can change scope: reassess the backlog and business case; confirm compliance requirements and put them in the backlog; do not release first and fix later.
  15. Control formally even when the change is good. Baseline changes in predictive work go through change control; adaptive change flows through the backlog, with contract thresholds respected.
  16. Do not close a phase on technical completion alone: formal acceptance and transition readiness (for example, trained support staff) come first.

13Exam Q&A

13.1 Scenario questions (choose the best answer)

S1Interviews with warehouse staff about a new picking app produce vague answers, because the pickers cannot explain how they actually work. Which elicitation technique would uncover the real requirements for the backlog?

  • AObservation and conversation, such as job shadowing while the pickers work
  • BA focus group led by the warehouse manager to discuss the new picking system
  • CA larger survey sent to all warehouse staff about their preferences for the system
  • DBenchmarking against the picking systems used by comparable companies
Show the answer

Answer: A. Observation and conversation (job shadowing) suits users who cannot or will not articulate their needs and reveals hidden requirements. Surveys, manager-led focus groups and benchmarking rely on what people say or on other organizations' practice.

S2In a backlog-refinement workshop, a senior director dominates the discussion and the other participants stay silent. Which technique would draw out everyone's ideas?

  • AA longer open brainstorming session with exactly the same participants
  • BA majority vote on the director's proposal at the start of the workshop
  • CNominal group technique, where everyone contributes ideas before discussion begins
  • DInterviews held with the director first, followed by a summary for the others
Show the answer

Answer: C. The nominal group technique gathers ideas from each person before any discussion, which equalizes participation and limits dominant voices. A vote on the director's proposal, more open discussion or director-first interviews keep the imbalance.

S3A review of the WBS shows every product deliverable but no entries for project management, testing or training work. What should the project manager do?

  • ACover the missing work later in the schedule without adding WBS elements
  • BAdd the work to the budget as a lump sum for management activities
  • CLeave it out, since the WBS should list only the customer's deliverables
  • DAdd the missing work, since the WBS must contain all product and project work
Show the answer

Answer: D. The 100% rule means the WBS contains all the product and project work, including project management, and nothing more. Omitting it, handling it only in the schedule or burying it in a lump sum leaves work outside the scope baseline.

S4A team has decomposed the WBS into two-hour tasks for a 14-month project, and the roll-up is hard to maintain. What is the better approach?

  • AStop at work packages that can be estimated, assigned and controlled
  • BDecompose further so that every task is shorter than one hour
  • CMerge the work into a few large deliverables with no work packages
  • DKeep the detail and add a second WBS to give managers a summary view
Show the answer

Answer: A. Decomposition continues only to the level where components are necessary and sufficient and can be estimated, assigned and controlled; too much detail wastes effort and creates roll-up problems. More detail, no work packages or a duplicate structure does not fix that.

S5A subcontractor asks exactly what is included in work package 3.2.1, who is responsible for it and how it will be accepted. Which document answers these questions?

  • AThe requirements traceability matrix, which links each need to a deliverable
  • BThe WBS dictionary, with each component's work, owner and acceptance criteria
  • CThe project charter, which records the high-level requirements and milestones
  • DThe WBS itself, which lists every component and shows its position in the hierarchy
Show the answer

Answer: B. The WBS dictionary supplies the detail behind each WBS component: description of work, responsible organization, schedule milestones, cost, quality requirements and acceptance criteria. The WBS shows structure only, the charter is high level, and the matrix links requirements to deliverables.

S6Of 50 planned scope items, the team correctly delivered 45 by the end of the phase. What is the scope definition accuracy?

  • A10%, because that is the share of the 50 planned items that were missed
  • B111%, because the 50 planned items divided by the 45 delivered gives 1.11
  • C90%, because 45 divided by 50 planned items, times 100, gives 90
  • D45%, because the delivered items are taken as a share of 100 items
Show the answer

Answer: C. Scope definition accuracy is the planned scope items correctly delivered divided by the total planned scope items, times 100: 45 divided by 50 gives 90%. The 10% figure is the share missed, 111% inverts the ratio, and 45% ignores the 50-item base.

S7The sponsor warns that funding may be cut and asks which top-level deliverables carry the most value so that they can be protected. Which scope tool helps most?

  • AA requirements traceability matrix listing each requirement's source and owner
  • BA Gantt chart showing which of the deliverables will finish first
  • CA work breakdown structure showing only the hierarchy of deliverables and work
  • DA value breakdown structure linking deliverables to their share of the intended value
Show the answer

Answer: D. A value breakdown structure links scope to intended value, giving top-level deliverables a value estimate that helps prioritize work. The WBS, the traceability matrix and a Gantt chart show structure, origin or sequence, not value.

S8Customers keep asking for mobile support that the team says was obviously never planned, but neither the scope statement nor the product backlog says so. What should the project manager do?

  • ARecord the mobile requests as risks and revisit them at the end of the project
  • BAdd mobile support to the scope to avoid any further disagreement with customers
  • CTell the customers that items which are not written down are never part of the project
  • DAdd explicit exclusions to the scope statement and review them with stakeholders
Show the answer

Answer: D. Exclusions in the project scope statement manage expectations and reduce scope creep, so what is out of scope is written down and agreed with stakeholders. Giving in, dismissing the requests or logging them as risks leaves the boundary unclear.

S9In the last iteration, 15 low-value stories remain in the backlog, and a stakeholder demands that all of them be delivered before the project can close. What is the best response?

  • ADeliver all of the stories before closure, because the backlog represents the agreed scope
  • BExplain that the main goals matter, and let the product owner rank the rest by value
  • CDelete the stories from the backlog without telling the stakeholder
  • DExtend the project until every story has been built and accepted
Show the answer

Answer: B. In adaptive work the team delivers the main product goals rather than every story on the list, and the product owner orders and trims the remainder by value. Delivering everything, deleting items silently or extending the project ignores the value-based approach.

S10A project manager asks the sponsor to approve the scope baseline, but the package contains only a WBS. What is missing?

  • AThe project scope statement and the WBS dictionary
  • BThe schedule baseline and the cost baseline
  • CThe project charter and the business case
  • DThe requirements traceability matrix and the risk register
Show the answer

Answer: A. In a predictive project the scope baseline is the approved scope statement, WBS and WBS dictionary, changeable only through formal change control. The charter, matrix, risk register and other baselines are different documents.

13.2 Recall Q&As

R1Name the six Scope processes.

Show the answer

Plan Scope Management, Elicit and Analyze Requirements, Define Scope, Develop Scope Structure, Monitor and Control Scope, Validate Scope.

R2Product scope versus project scope?

Show the answer

Product scope is the features, functions and characteristics of the product, service or result. Project scope is the work performed to deliver it.

R3What forms the scope baseline, and what replaces it in adaptive work?

Show the answer

Predictive: project scope statement + WBS + WBS dictionary, changed through formal change control. Adaptive: the prioritized backlog, baselined at the start of each iteration, with the product owner approving changes.

R4What does the project scope statement contain?

Show the answer

Scope description, deliverables, acceptance criteria and exclusions (with assumptions and constraints).

R5What is the 100% rule?

Show the answer

The WBS includes all product and project work (including project management) and nothing more; lower levels roll up to the higher.

R6Define work package, planning package and control account.

Show the answer

Work package: lowest WBS level, estimable and controllable. Planning package: known content, no detailed activities yet. Control account: management control point integrating scope, budget and schedule.

R7What does the WBS dictionary hold?

Show the answer

Per WBS element: identifier, description, assumptions and constraints, responsible organization, milestones, activities, resources, cost, quality requirements, acceptance criteria, technical references and agreement information.

R8What is the requirements traceability matrix for?

Show the answer

To link each requirement from its origin to the deliverable that satisfies it, proving every approved requirement is delivered and adds business value, and structuring product-scope change management.

R9Verify versus validate?

Show the answer

Verification (Monitor and Control Scope) checks compliance with requirements and standards and produces verified deliverables. Validation (Validate Scope) obtains formal customer acceptance and produces accepted deliverables.

R10What is scope creep?

Show the answer

Uncontrolled expansion of scope without adjusting time, cost and resources.

R11What do the letters in MoSCoW stand for?

Show the answer

Must have, should have, could have, will not have.

R12Definition of done versus acceptance criteria?

Show the answer

The DoD is the checklist of criteria any item must meet to be ready for use or release; acceptance criteria are the conditions for accepting a particular deliverable or story.

R13Name the requirement classifications in PMBOK 8.

Show the answer

Business, stakeholder, solution (functional and nonfunctional), transition and readiness, project and quality requirements.

R14Who approves scope changes in adaptive work?

Show the answer

Usually the product owner, dynamically through the backlog, without a formal change control procedure (unless a contract or governance threshold requires formal approval).

14Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Domain goal All the work required, and only the work required; quality is part of scope
Six processes Plan Scope Mgmt → Elicit and Analyze Requirements → Define Scope → Develop Scope Structure → Monitor and Control Scope → Validate Scope
Scope baseline Scope statement + WBS + WBS dictionary (predictive); with schedule and cost baselines = PMB
Adaptive scope Prioritized backlog; baseline per iteration; product owner approves; DoD
Scope statement Description, deliverables, acceptance criteria, exclusions (+ assumptions, constraints)
Charter vs scope statement High level vs detailed
WBS Deliverable-oriented; 100% rule; work packages estimable and controllable; planning packages for far work
WBS dictionary Detail per WBS element (owner, resources, cost, quality, acceptance criteria)
Requirements Business, stakeholder, solution (functional, nonfunctional), transition, project, quality; unambiguous, traceable, complete, consistent, acceptable
RTM Origin → deliverable → test → acceptance; shows every requirement delivered
Elicitation Interviews, focus groups, surveys, observation, benchmarking, brainstorming, nominal group, document analysis, design thinking, prototypes
Prioritization MoSCoW, 100-point, cost of delay, Kano; adaptive: by value
Verify vs validate Verified deliverables (team, correctness) vs accepted deliverables (customer, formal)
Scope creep Uncontrolled growth without adjusting time, cost, resources; gold plating Beyond PMBOK 8
In scope but missing from WBS Add to WBS; no change request
Free extra / upgrade Assess impact and use change control
Metrics (Table 2-6) Scope definition accuracy; scope creep % = unplanned ÷ total; requirements stability = unchanged ÷ total (PMBOK prints the last two inverted)
MVP Fewest features that deliver value in a first release
First-action pattern Check the baseline and requirements, surface conflicts and expectations, trace, then change control (predictive) or backlog and product owner (adaptive)
